questions.question: What is added to the real number system to form the extended real number system?
Why are $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ added in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ rather than treated as ordinary real numbers?
options: They are the largest and smallest elements of $\mathbb{R}$.
They are limits of real sequences, so they must be real.
They are order endpoints, not finite real values.
They are irrational reals too large to write down.

questions.question: Which interval notation is also used for the extended real number system?
Which object is an element added beyond ordinary real numbers in this extension?
How should infinities be understood?
options: As the largest ordinary real numbers
As symbols rather than big numbers

questions.question: Why is the extended real number system useful?
options: It makes arithmetic such as $+\infty-(+\infty)$ well defined.
It unifies limits, divergence, and unbounded behaviour.
It turns every divergent sequence into a convergent one.
It gives every subset of $\mathbb{R}$ a maximum and a minimum.

questions.question: Which notation best represents a limit value in the extended real numbers but not in ordinary $\mathbb{R}$?
If a discussion allows the value $+\infty$ for a limit statement, which number system is being used?
Which statement avoids a common misconception about $+\infty$?
options: $+\infty$ is the real number reached as the limit of $a_n=n$.
$+\infty$ is a symbol of $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, not a real number.

questions.question: Since $\infty$ is not a real number, unbounded limits require an extended set. Which relationship holds between $\mathbb{R}$ and $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$?
options: $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ replaces every real by its reciprocal.

questions.question: Which proposed notation is consistent for the extended real system?
A student says, '$+\infty$ belongs to $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, so it is just a very large real number.' What is the best correction?
options: It is not in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, which contains only the real numbers.
It belongs as an added symbol, not a real number.
It is a real number, but larger than every natural number.
It is a real number only when it arises as a limit.

questions.question: What is the extended real number system?
options: The real numbers together with $+\infty$ only.
The real numbers together with $+\infty$ and $-\infty$.
The real numbers together with the complex numbers.
The rational numbers together with $+\infty$ and $-\infty$.

questions.question: How should $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ be understood in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$?
options: As the largest and smallest integers.
As very large reals that obey ordinary arithmetic.
As the limits of every unbounded real sequence.
As symbols, not ordinary large real numbers.

questions.question: Which notation denotes the extended real number system?
Which object is in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ but not in ordinary $\mathbb{R}$?
Which notation represents the interval form of the extended real number system?
A limit statement has value $-\infty$. Which framework naturally includes that value?
Why is $[-\infty,+\infty]$ only an interval-form notation, rather than an ordinary real interval?
options: Because $\pm\infty$ are symbols, not real endpoints.
Because it must equal $(-\infty,+\infty)$, so the brackets are wrong.
Because an interval cannot contain infinitely many reals.
Because $\pm\infty$ belong to $\mathbb{R}$ but not to $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$.
